title: Indian Architecture as Tourist Attractions
summary: Indian architecture grew through the ages under dynasties, regional traditions and external influences, and shows the cultural diversity of the country. Order: Harappan, Vedic, Buddhist and Jain, Mauryan, Gupta, rock-cut and free-standing temples, medieval Indo-Islamic (Sultanate, regional kingdoms, Mughal) and colonial and modern styles.

Harappan cities (Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Kalibangan, Surkotada, Lothal) had grid-pattern town planning, roads cutting at right angles, a citadel on high ground, an advanced drainage system, public baths, pillared halls and dwelling houses of well-baked bricks laid in gypsum mortar that survived five thousand years. Lothal (Gujarat) has a dockyard. The bronze dancing girl of Mohenjodaro and a terracotta yogic figure show sculpting skill. The Vedic Aryans used wood, bamboo and reeds (so nothing survives); their most important feature was the fire altar; they used wood along with brick and stone.

Buddhists and Jains built stupas, viharas (monasteries) and chaityas (congregational halls). Buddha's four stupa sites: Lumbini (birth), Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon) and Kushinagar (Mahaparinirvana). Under the Mauryas (322–182 BCE) and Ashoka, polished monolithic stone pillars with animal capitals carried the Dhamma; each weighs about 50 tonnes and stands about 50 ft; the lion capital of the Sarnath pillar is the national emblem. The stupas of Sanchi and Sarnath symbolise Mauryan achievement; Sanchi's gateways show Jataka scenes. Gandhara art blended Greek and Indian art. Nagarjunakonda is another Buddhist site. More than a thousand caves were excavated between the 2nd century BCE and 10th century CE (Ajanta, Ellora, Udaygiri). Rock-cut temples: the chaitya at Karle, the Kailash temple at Ellora (Rashtrakutas) and the ratha temples of Mahabalipuram (Pallavas).

Free-standing Hindu temples began in the Gupta period (Deogarh, Bhitargaon) with a garbhagriha. Dravida style (south): vimana or shikhara, high walls and a gopuram gateway; Pallava shore temple at Mahabalipuram, Kailashnath and Vaikuntha Perumal at Kanchipuram, the Chola Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore, Belur and Halebid. Nagara style (north and east): shikharas (spiral roofs), garbhagriha and mandap; Lingaraja, Mukteshwara and Jagannath (Odisha); the Sun Temple at Konark (13th century, Narasimha Deva I, a twelve-wheeled chariot for Surya); the Khajuraho temples (Chandellas, 10th–11th century, Kandariya Mahadev). Dilwara temples at Mount Abu (Jain, white marble, Solanki patronage).

The Turks brought domes, arches and minarets and used local craftsmen, so Islamic and indigenous styles blended. Delhi Sultanate: Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and Qutub Minar (70 m, five storeys), Alai Darwaza and Hauz Khas (Alauddin Khalji), the strong Tughlaq forts and tombs, the tombs of Ibrahim Lodi and Sher Shah (Sasaram). Regional kingdoms: Ahmedabad (Jama Masjid, Sidi Saiyyad), Mandu (Jahaz Mahal, Hindola Mahal), Deccan (Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur has the largest dome; Golconda fort), Bengal (Adina mosque), Jaunpur (Atala mosque), Hampi of Vijayanagar.

Mughals: Humayun's Tomb (red stone, in a garden, precursor of the Taj), Akbar's forts at Agra and Fatehpur Sikri with the Buland Darwaza (about 41 m, built after the Gujarat victory), Itimad-ud-daula's marble tomb, and Shah Jahan's marble buildings with pietra dura inlay: the Red Fort, Jama Masjid and the Taj Mahal (dome, four minarets, gateway and gardens). Mughal gardens: Shalimar at Kashmir and Lahore.

Portuguese churches in Goa (Basilica of Bom Jesus, St Francis); British Greek and Roman colonnades (Parliament House, Connaught Place), Rashtrapati Bhavan by Lutyens (sandstone with jaali and canopies), the Victoria Memorial (marble, now a museum) and Writers' Building in Kolkata, St Paul's Cathedral (Gothic), Victoria Terminus (now Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus) and the Gateway of India (Indo-Saracenic, yellow basalt, 1924) in Mumbai. After 1947: Le Corbusier designed Chandigarh; Joseph Allen Stein designed the India International Centre; modern Indian architects include Raj Rewal and Charles Correa.

Town planning goes back to about 2350 BCE. There were 2,837 towns in 1594 (qasbas as small towns). The British built port towns (Panaji 1510, Bombay 1532, Madras 1639, Calcutta 1690), railways from 1853, hill stations (Mussoorie, Shimla, Nainital, Darjeeling, Shillong, Nilgiris, Kodaikanal) and Civil Lines and cantonments. Delhi has at least seven old cities: Indraprastha (Yudhishthira), Lal Kot (Anang Pal Tomar), Mehrauli (Prithviraj Chauhan), Siri (Alauddin Khalji), Tughlaqabad (Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq), Jahanpanah (Muhammad bin Tughlaq), Firozabad (Firoz Shah), Dinpanah (Humayun) and Shahjahanabad (Shah Jahan). It became the capital of British India in 1911 and New Delhi was completed by 1932. Howrah Bridge (over the Hooghly) is a symbol of Kolkata; Mumbai's Gateway of India and CST and Chennai's High Court, Fort St George and Church of St John are tourist sites.

objective: Fill in the blanks. (a) The Buddha's burial mounds built at Lumbini, Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar are called ________. (b) The Gateway of India in Mumbai was completed in ________ in the Indo-Saracenic style.
(a) Stupas. (b) 1924.

Fill in the blanks. (a) A very exciting place for tourists to visit are the sites of the ________ valley civilization. (b) The stupas of Sanchi and Sarnath are symbols of the achievement of ________ architecture.
(a) Indus. (b) Mauryan.

(a) Dhamma. (b) National emblem.

(a) False: they used wood, bamboo and reeds, so no Vedic structure survives. (b) True.

(a) True. (b) False: it was built in red stone.

vsa: Explain any two characteristics of rock-cut temples.
They were cut out of the rock, as at Karle, Ellora's Kailash temple and Mahabalipuram's rathas, and the stability of rock attracted patrons. They were decorated with beautiful sculptures.
April 2025
Explain the systematic evolution of Indian architecture in two points.

Indian architecture grew from Harappan town planning through Buddhist, Mauryan and Gupta temples to medieval Indo-Islamic styles. It was shaped by dynasties, regions and external influences, ending in colonial and modern styles.
October 2025
Describe the fire altars, the most important feature of Vedic architecture.
The Vedic Aryans built courtyards and mandaps with altars for worship of fire. Fire altars remain important in Hindu homes and marriages, but no Vedic structure survives because wood was used.
April 2024

or: Describe two main characteristics of the beautiful temples of Odisha.
They follow the Nagara style with shikharas, a garbhagriha and a mandap. Examples are the Lingaraja, Mukteshwara and Jagannath temples and the Konark Sun Temple, a twelve-wheeled chariot.

vsa: Describe the town planning of the Harappan cities in two points.
Cities were built on a grid pattern with roads that cut each other at right angles. They had a citadel on high ground, an advanced drainage system and houses of well-baked bricks.
Mention any two features of Mauryan architecture.
Highly polished monolithic stone pillars with animal capitals carried Ashoka's teachings. Stupas such as those at Sanchi and Sarnath show Mauryan skill.
What is the Dravida style of architecture?
It is the South Indian temple style developed by the Cholas with a vimana or shikhara, high walls and a gateway topped with a gopuram.
What is pietra dura?
It is decorative inlay work in stones, used in the Mughal buildings of Shah Jahan, such as the Taj Mahal.
Name the two Buddhist architectural forms and state their use.
A stupa is a mound built over Buddha's relics and at sites of his life events. A vihara is a monastery and a chaitya is a congregational hall for preaching and teaching.
Why is Howrah Bridge a symbol of Kolkata? Give two points.
It crosses the Hooghly river and connects Howrah to Kolkata. It stands on two 270 ft pillars and was built without nuts and bolts, being probably the busiest bridge in the world.
sa: Analyse the impacts of the British on Indian architecture in three points.

(i) Greek and Roman colonnaded buildings such as Parliament House and Connaught Place were built. (ii) Gothic and Indo-Saracenic buildings appeared, such as St Paul's Cathedral, Victoria Terminus and the Gateway of India, along with Lutyens's Rashtrapati Bhavan combining jaali and canopies. (iii) New cities, ports, railway terminals, hill stations, Civil Lines and cantonments were planned.
Explain any three characteristics of burial mounds (stupas).

(i) Stupas were huge mud mounds enclosed in burnt bricks, built where Buddha's remains were kept. (ii) They stand at his birthplace Lumbini, Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar. (iii) Viharas and chaityas grew around them and they became tourist landmarks.
Explain the contribution of the Gupta, Pallava and Chola rulers to temple architecture (three points).

(i) The Guptas began free-standing temples with a garbhagriha (Deogarh, Bhitargaon). (ii) The Pallavas built the Shore temple, rathas and Kanchipuram temples. (iii) The Cholas built the Brihadeshwara temple and developed the Dravida style with vimana and gopuram.
Explain the Mughal style of architecture (three points).

(i) Humayun's Tomb, Agra and Fatehpur Sikri with the Buland Darwaza show a synthesis of Persian and Indian elements. (ii) Shah Jahan used marble and pietra dura in the Red Fort, Jama Masjid and the Taj Mahal. (iii) Gardens around tombs, such as Shalimar, were a unique development.
Describe the architecture of the Delhi Sultanate (three points).

(i) Turks brought domes, arches and minarets and used local craftsmen, blending Islamic and Indian styles. (ii) Qutub Minar (70 m), Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and Alai Darwaza are examples. (iii) Tughlaq buildings had massive, strong walls because of Mongol threats.
la: Explain the architectural styles from the Harappan period to the Gupta period in six points.

(i) Harappan cities had grid planning, drains, public baths and brick houses. (ii) The Vedic period used wood and fire altars. (iii) Buddhist and Jain stupas, viharas and chaityas appeared. (iv) Mauryan polished pillars and the Sanchi and Sarnath stupas, with the lion capital as national emblem. (v) Cave architecture at Ajanta, Ellora and Udaygiri, and rock-cut temples at Karle. (vi) Gupta period began free-standing temples at Deogarh and Bhitargaon.
Describe the contribution of Buddhism and Jainism to Indian architecture and the regional temple styles, in six points.

(i) Buddhists built stupas at Lumbini, Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar. (ii) Viharas and chaityas became centres of teaching. (iii) Caves of Ajanta and Ellora hold Buddhist halls. (iv) Dilwara Jain temples at Mount Abu are built in white marble. (v) The Dravida style of the South has vimana and gopuram. (vi) The Nagara style of the North and East has shikhara, garbhagriha and mandap (Konark, Khajuraho).
The architecture of the Mughal period was a synthesis of Indian, Persian and Central Asian styles. Explain in six points.

(i) Humayun's Tomb in red stone with a garden is a precursor of the Taj. (ii) Akbar built the forts at Agra and Fatehpur Sikri. (iii) The Buland Darwaza (41 m) reflects Mughal grandeur. (iv) Jahangir built Akbar's mausoleum and the marble tomb of Itimad-ud-daula. (v) Shah Jahan used marble and pietra dura in the Red Fort, Jama Masjid and the Taj Mahal. (vi) Living beings were carved in brackets and gardens such as Shalimar were laid.
